title: PB-LLM: Partially Binarized Large Language Models
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of compressing large language models (LLMs) to extremely low bit-widths while preserving their reasoning and language performance. The authors argue that existing binarization methods collapse when applied directly to LLMs, and that standard aggressive quantization methods lose quality beyond 4 bits. Their goal is to make 1-bit or near-1-bit LLMs feasible for efficient deployment.

The proposed approach, PB-LLM (Partially-Binarized LLM), keeps a small fraction of salient weights in higher precision while binarizing the rest. The paper studies how to identify salient weights using magnitude or Hessian-based criteria, compares element-wise versus column-wise selection, and then develops two training/quantization strategies: PB-GPTQ for post-training quantization and a quantization-aware training (QAT) method that freezes salient weights and uses an analytically derived optimal scaling factor for binary weights.

Experiments are conducted on pretrained OPT-1.3B and LLaMA-7B models, using large public text corpora for calibration/training and common-sense reasoning benchmarks such as BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and OBQA, as well as perplexity on C4 and WikiText2. The main conclusion is that partial binarization can substantially outperform naive binarization and that preserving even a small set of salient weights is critical for maintaining performance. The paper is a model-compression methods paper, not an educational intervention study, so no student/teacher population is reported.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a model-compression methods paper about partially binarized large language models, not an educational intervention study. It does not evaluate student learning, classroom use, or any K-12 educational outcome.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct educational impact assessed in the paper. Any relevance to education would be indirect and technical, through more efficient LLM deployment, but no K-12 outcome or subgroup/moderator evidence is reported.
